figures.label: fig:overview
figures.title: Overview: what the model takes, does and returns
figures.shows: A protein can stay almost the same between species while the cells use its gene differently, and a protein can change while the cells use it alike. Panel (a) shows these two cases with two toy genes: protein sequence on top, expression across cell states below. Panel (b) lists what the model is given: single-cell counts from several species for genes that have exactly one counterpart in each species, how similar the proteins are (the protein prior), and a description of each gene (protein language model, protein similarity, expression statistics). Panel (c) is the model. Cells of all species are placed on one map. Two decoders explain the counts together: one does not know the species, the other does. A gate per gene decides how much of the species-aware decoder is let in. The gate starts where the protein similarity puts it and moves only when the counts say so; that count evidence is called S_g. Panel (d) shows what comes out: the cell map, and for every gene the count evidence, the gate, and how far the gate ended from its protein-based start (Δα). Above the prior means the cells of the species share the gene's pattern; below means the pattern or the level differs. Genes with too few counts get a value from genes with similar proteins, shown in gray. Panel (e) lists what the paper does with these readouts.

figures.label: fig:alpha-intro
figures.title: The gate value α against the protein prior
figures.shows: Every dot or bar is a gene. The model starts each gene at a value set by how similar its protein is between the species (the protein prior). During training the gene's value α can move away from that start when the counts say so. (a) α against the prior: most genes stay near the diagonal and many leave it. (b) The move itself, Δα = α minus the prior: about half of the genes move up and half move down. (c) The distribution of α beside that of the prior: the same overall shape, shifted by the data.

figures.title: Training dynamics of α

figures.label: fig:supp-gate-gap
figures.title: Where the two readouts agree and differ
figures.shows: Chimera can read each gene in two ways: through the default protein-feature gate, where a network sets the gene's value from its protein features, and through the companion per-gene gate, where each gene gets its own value from its counts. Panel a takes one cohort, kidney from human and mouse, and plots the two readings against each other for the 9,042 genes with count evidence in both fits. Most genes lie along the diagonal (Spearman 0.63); the colored ones differ by more than the noise between training seeds, 430 higher from their own counts and 803 lower. Panel b repeats this for all 26 cohorts: how reproducible the difference is when the training seeds are split in two halves (0.47 to 0.99, against a band centered on zero when one gate's seeds are split), how strongly the two readings agree (0.30 to 0.79), and what share of genes is called different (0 to 32 %). Panel c asks whether proteins that look alike to a protein language model (the 15 nearest neighbors in ESM-2 space) are read alike: they share little of the per-gene reading (median 0.09) and much more of the protein-feature reading (median 0.19, up to 0.70), so the default gate reads a protein family as a unit and the per-gene read-out keeps its members apart. Panel d shows which gene properties go with the difference: the strongest is uneven detection between the species (partial correlation -0.23 to -0.56 in 21 of 26 cohorts), and all seven properties together explain 12 to 49 % of it.

figures.label: fig:supp-gate-gap-cont
figures.title: The difference between the readouts by tissue, gene class and independent reference
figures.checks: listed: letters, scale, spelling, text, words
figures.shows: This figure asks what the difference between the two readings of a gene is made of. Panel e compares cohorts in pairs: each reading is similar between cohorts of the same tissue (median Spearman 0.57 for the per-gene read-out, 0.54 for the protein-feature gate) and still related between tissues (0.20 and 0.25), while the difference is related within a tissue (0.24) and almost not between tissues (0.03). A gene accounts for 8 % of the variance of the difference across eight tissues, against 22 to 23 % for either reading: the difference belongs to a gene in a tissue. Panel f looks at whole gene classes. Mitochondrial proteins, the translation machinery, proliferation programs and protein homeostasis read higher from their counts than from their protein family in three or four of eight tissues; transcription factors, zinc-finger factors and receptors read lower. The two columns at the right show that both readings place these classes on the same side of the prior, the protein-feature gate further out. Panel g tests each reading against independent data while holding the other reading fixed: the per-gene read-out adds agreement on 26 of 32 gene-level references and on all nine held-out cortical regions (0.16 to 0.28), and the protein-feature gate still adds agreement on liver pattern and on fine kidney cell types. Panel h shows that the difference is unrelated to how constrained a gene's sequence is (dN/dS and LOEUF, all values between -0.07 and +0.10).

figures.label: fig:supp-e3-compartments
figures.title: Home compartments of genes against Δα
figures.shows: Every gene is given a "home": the cell type in which human cells use it most, or no home if it is used in all cells. Home cell types are grouped into four compartments: the specialized cells of a tissue (neurons, kidney tubule cells, germ cells), stromal cells, blood-vessel cells and immune cells. Panel (a) asks, for each compartment and each of the 26 cohorts, whether its genes score higher or lower than comparison genes with the same protein identity, expression, detection and cell-type specificity. Four scores stand side by side: Chimera's Δα with the default protein-feature gate, Δα read gene by gene, the correlation of cell-type expression profiles between species, and the similarity of expression level at the home cell type. Genes of specialized cells sit above their protein prior in 23 of 24 and 24 of 24 cohorts, while their expression level at the home cell type is the least similar between species (2 of 24 above zero); genes used in every cell show the reverse in 26 of 26 cohorts. Panel (b) splits the compartments into 70 finer cell groups from nine cohorts and plots how much the level differs between species against the per-gene Δα excess: specialized cell groups gather where both are positive, and the liver sinusoidal endothelium is the most shared program of all (+0.79 SD).

figures.label: fig:supp-e3-lineages
figures.title: Cell types that carry shared deployment

Genes of the liver sinusoidal endothelium (the lining of the liver's blood channels) are the most shared program of any tissue, +0.79 to +1.19 SD in all four liver models, while hepatocyte genes sit near their prior. In the eye, genes of the trabecular meshwork (the tissue through which fluid leaves the eye, central to glaucoma), ciliary muscle and Schwann cells are above; in the cortex, the neurons; in the testis, spermatocytes and spermatids. Panel (b) names seven genes for four of these cell types and shows their per-gene Δα as a z-score in every model of the tissue: a row that is red in every column is a gene above its prior whichever species set was used. Examples are HEG1 and PLXND1 in the liver endothelium, the glaucoma gene MYOC in the trabecular meshwork, and ANK3 and GAP43 in neurons.

figures.label: fig:supp-e3-primates
figures.title: Species-specific departures along the primate phylogeny
figures.shows: One model was fitted to prefrontal cortex cells of four primates at once: human, chimpanzee, macaque and marmoset. For every gene and cell type the model gives each species its own evidence value, and a species "departs" when its value is clearly lower than those of the other three. Panel (a) plots how often each species departs against the length of its own branch of the primate tree: about 9 to 11 % of gene-by-cell-type pairs for human and chimpanzee (6.4 million years), 13 % for macaque (28.8) and 24 % for marmoset (43). Both gates of Chimera and a direct comparison of expression levels give the same order. Panel (b) tests this in a second cortical region from another laboratory that the model never saw: genes that depart more on the marmoset branch than on the macaque branch also show the larger expression gap there (ρ = 0.17), and departures on the human branch agree with a human-specific gap (ρ = 0.07), with the chimpanzee branch as a control. Panel (c) shows five genes that an earlier study reported as changed on the human lineage: in the cell type named by that study the human bar lies below those of the other three primates, for example FOXP2 in microglia.

(b) and (c): how strongly the output reacts to a small change of an input, per group and with sign for the eight single numbers. The figure asks whether genes that are neighbors there also get similar values from the model, for four liver cohorts from a close pair of species to four species. Solid bars are the measured agreement between a gene and its 15 protein neighbors; the other bars are two chance levels (values shuffled among genes; random numbers in place of the protein description). Top row: agreement as a rank correlation for (a) α, (b) Δα, (c) the protein prior. Bottom row: the same with a second statistic, Moran's I, for (d) α, (e) Δα, (f) the prior.

figures.label: fig:supp-esm2-umap-archetype-trajectory
figures.title: Δα of the archetypes during training
figures.shows: The gate network sorts genes into three groups by its own internal description of them (the archetypes A0, A1, A2 of the main atlas figure). The figure follows the mean Δα of each group while the four-species liver model trains. All three start at zero, because the gate starts at the prior, and separate after about 20 epochs: A0 ends clearly below the prior, A1 slightly below, A2 above.

figures.label: fig:supp-esm2-umap-archetype-enrichment
figures.title: Gene categories enriched in the archetypes
figures.shows: The three gene groups found inside the gate network (archetypes A0, A1, A2) are compared with groups of genes defined by function, on the four-species liver model. Red means that a functional group has more genes in an archetype than expected by chance, blue fewer; a star marks the cells that pass the statistical test. (a) 35 fine groups, (b) ten broad groups; each map has its own color scale.

figures.label: fig:supp-gin-protein-residue-beta
figures.title: Residue-level mixed-effects regression
figures.shows: For 70 proteins the sensitivity of the model can be traced to single amino-acid positions (36,832 in all). A statistical model asks which properties of a position go with higher sensitivity when all other properties are held equal and differences between proteins are set aside. Each bar is one property with its 95% interval; bars to the right mean higher sensitivity; dark bars are statistically supported. The effects are small.

figures.label: fig:supp-gin-protein-cliffs-delta
figures.title: Protein-replicated effect sizes of residue features
figures.shows: Twenty comparisons between kinds of amino-acid positions (for example exposed against buried, hydrophobic against charged), each asking which kind receives more of the model's sensitivity. The bar is the size of the difference with its interval. Two tests are given per row: one that pools all positions, and a stricter one that compares the two kinds inside each protein and asks whether the proteins agree. Filled bars pass the stricter test.

figures.label: fig:supp-gin-protein-attention-by-feature
figures.title: Per-residue attribution by structural feature
figures.shows: The size of the model's sensitivity at each of the 36,832 amino-acid positions of 70 proteins, as box plots (line: median, box: middle half), grouped four ways: (a) by the local shape of the chain, (b) by how buried the position is, (c) by how confident the predicted structure is there, (d) by the chemistry of the amino acid. The boxes overlap almost completely; the number of positions is given under each box.

figures.shows: One protein, ETV1 (a protein that the model leaves at its prior, with protein-language and expression inputs in balance), read along its chain from the first to the last amino acid. From top to bottom: where the proteins of macaque, mouse and zebrafish differ from the human one; how much the protein language model sees the species differ at each position; how unusual each position is within the protein; a combined relevance score; and how strongly each position pushes the model's value for this gene up or down. The strip at the bottom gives the share of the model's sensitivity for this gene by kind of input.
